core.text: A Latin verb carries its own subject in its ending: **the person endings (I / you / he / we / you all / they on the verb)**. *-ō* I, *-s* you, *-t* he / she / it, *-mus* we, *-tis* you all, *-nt* they. So *dormiō* is *I sleep*, *dormīs* *you sleep*, then *dormit, dormīmus, dormītis, dormiunt*. Between stem and ending sits the conjugation's vowel: *clāmā-s, rīdē-s, dīc-i-s, audī-s*; the 3rd conjugation has *-u-* before *-nt* (*dīcunt, faciunt*). Because the ending says who, *ego* and *tū* appear only for emphasis. Latin name: dēsinentiae persōnālēs āctīvae.
Person is who is talking: first person = the speaker (I, we), second = the listener (you), third = anyone else. English shows it only in *am / are / is* and *he sleeps*.
-ō, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt; the vowel in front belongs to the conjugation.

Each active ending has a passive twin: *-ō / -or*, *-s / -ris*, *-t / -tur*, *-mus / -mur*, *-tis / -minī*, *-nt / -ntur*: *laudō* I praise, *laudor* I am praised. A final *r* (or *-minī*) means the subject is on the receiving end, or the verb is a deponent (looks passive, means active).

more.text: The 1st conjugation drops its *a* before *-ō*: *clāmā-re* but *clām-ō*. Outside the present tense the first person ends in *-m* instead of *-ō*: *sum, eram, dīcam* — so *-m* is the *I* ending everywhere else.

Your notes: the endings are *-ō / -m, -(i)s, -(i)t, -(i)mus, -(i)tis, -(u)nt*; the bracketed vowel appears where the stem ends in a consonant (*frang-is, frang-imus, frang-itis*) and not after *a-, e-* and *i-*stems (*ambulā-s, tenē-mus, audī-tis*); in the present indicative only *-ō* is used for *I*, and *a-*stems drop their *a* before it (*ambul-ō*) because two open vowels are hard to say together. The nominative pronouns *ego, tū, is* are redundant and mark emphasis, as English does with the voice, so *ambulō* is far commoner than *ego ambulō*.

Ørberg (chapter XV): persōna prīma *rīdeō rīdēmus*, secunda *rīdēs rīdētis*, tertia *rīdet rīdent*; *clāmō clāmāmus, dīcō dīcimus, faciō facimus, audiō audīmus*; and beside them *esse* (*sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt*), *īre* (*eō, īs, it, īmus, ītis, eunt*) and *posse* (*possum, potes, potest, possumus, potestis, possunt*).
